timeline.title: Born in Smiljan
timeline.text: Nikola Tesla was born in Smiljan, in the Military Frontier of the Austrian Empire. The village is now in Croatia. He was the fourth of five children of a priest and a mother who made her own household tools.

timeline.title: Nine months of illness
timeline.text: He finished high school at 17, then caught cholera and was bedridden for nine months. His father, who had wanted him to become a priest, promised to send him to engineering school if he recovered.

timeline.title: Engineering school in Graz
timeline.text: He enrolled at the Imperial-Royal Technical College in Graz on a scholarship. Watching a direct current machine spark at its brushes in class, he wondered if a motor could run without them. He left in December 1878 without a degree.

timeline.title: First job in electrical work
timeline.text: He moved to Budapest to work for Tivadar Puskas on a new telephone exchange. He started as a draftsman at the Central Telegraph Office and became chief electrician when the exchange opened.

timeline.title: The rotating magnetic field
timeline.text: Tesla said the idea of a rotating magnetic field came to him on a walk in a Budapest park, and that he drew the diagrams in the sand. This date and story come from his own later account.

timeline.title: Working for Continental Edison
timeline.text: Puskas found him a job with the Continental Edison Company near Paris, installing electric lighting. Managers soon had him designing improved dynamos and motors.

timeline.title: Arrives in America
timeline.text: Tesla moved to the United States in June 1884 and began work at the Edison Machine Works in Manhattan. He troubleshot installations and improved generators.

timeline.title: Leaves the Edison company
timeline.text: He quit after about six months. The reason is unclear. In his autobiography he said a promised 50,000 dollar bonus turned out to be a joke, but historians note the company did not have that much cash on hand.

timeline.title: His own lighting company
timeline.text: Two businessmen backed the Tesla Electric Light and Manufacturing Company to make arc lighting. Tesla built and installed the system in Rahway, New Jersey, and won his first US patents, granted from January 1886.

timeline.title: Pushed out and penniless
timeline.text: The investors dropped the manufacturing business and formed a new utility without him. He had assigned his patents to the company, so he lost them. He took repair jobs and dug ditches for 2 dollars a day.

timeline.title: The AC induction motor
timeline.text: His induction motor, which ran on alternating current and needed no brushes, was patented on 1 May 1888. On 16 May he demonstrated it at the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. Galileo Ferraris had presented a similar motor in Italy in March 1888.

timeline.title: Westinghouse licenses the motor
timeline.text: George Westinghouse licensed his polyphase motor and transformer patents for 60,000 dollars in cash and stock plus a royalty per horsepower. Tesla spent a year in Pittsburgh as a consultant, a time he found frustrating.

timeline.title: Giving up his royalties
timeline.text: Westinghouse Electric was in financial trouble after the panic of 1890. In early 1891 Tesla agreed to release the company from the per-motor royalty in his contract.

timeline.title: The Tesla coil goes public
timeline.text: After learning of Heinrich Hertz's radio wave experiments in 1889, he designed a new high frequency transformer. In a lecture at Columbia College before the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, he first showed his resonant transformer, the Tesla coil, and lit gas tubes without wires. He patented the coil circuit that year.

timeline.title: Becomes a US citizen
timeline.text: Tesla became a naturalized citizen of the United States at age 35.

timeline.title: Lecturing in Europe
timeline.text: He gave his lecture 'Experiments with Alternate Currents of High Potential and High Frequency' before the Institution of Electrical Engineers in London. From 1892 to 1894 he also served as a vice-president of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers.

timeline.title: Talks of signals without wires
timeline.text: In lectures at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia and in St. Louis, he said a system like his could one day send signals, or even power, to any distance without wires.

timeline.title: AC lights the World's Fair
timeline.text: Westinghouse lit the World's Columbian Exposition with alternating current and showed Tesla's motors, including a spinning copper 'Egg of Columbus'. Tesla gave demonstrations of wireless lighting in a darkened room.

timeline.title: Advice for Niagara
timeline.text: Asked how to send power from Niagara Falls, Tesla advised a two-phase alternating current system. Westinghouse won the contract to build the generating system there.

timeline.title: Fire destroys his lab
timeline.text: The building on South Fifth Avenue that held his lab caught fire. His notes, models and demonstration pieces, including many shown at the 1893 fair, were destroyed, and his projects were set back.

timeline.title: X-ray experiments
timeline.text: After Wilhelm Roentgen announced X-rays, Tesla built his own X-ray tubes powered by his coil. He noted the skin damage they caused, though he wrongly blamed ozone rather than the rays.

timeline.title: A boat steered by radio
timeline.text: At an electrical exhibition in Madison Square Garden he showed a boat controlled by radio, which he called a telautomaton. He offered it to the US military as a torpedo, but they showed little interest.

timeline.title: Lightning in Colorado
timeline.text: He set up a high-altitude lab to test sending power without wires. His giant coil made artificial lightning, with discharges he and others reported at over 100 feet. He concluded, wrongly, that the whole Earth could carry electrical energy.

timeline.title: An essay on human energy
timeline.text: The Century Magazine published his long article 'The Problem of Increasing Human Energy'. It read more as a philosophical essay than a clear account of his experiments.

timeline.title: Morgan funds a wireless station
timeline.text: Financier J. P. Morgan agreed to give him 150,000 dollars for a wireless station on Long Island, in return for a 51 percent share of the patents. This became Wardenclyffe Tower.

timeline.title: Marconi crosses the Atlantic first
timeline.text: Tesla had already enlarged his plans and asked Morgan for more money, which was refused. In December 1901 Guglielmo Marconi sent a radio signal across the Atlantic, beating him to it.

timeline.title: Morgan says no
timeline.text: Morgan replied that he would not make any further advances. Other investors stayed away, and money kept running short.

timeline.title: Wardenclyffe stops
timeline.text: His alternating current patents expired in May 1905, ending royalty income. Work at Wardenclyffe came to a halt. Sources differ on the year: one says 1905, another says the site was abandoned in 1906.

timeline.title: The bladeless turbine
timeline.text: On his 50th birthday he demonstrated a bladeless turbine of 200 horsepower running at 16,000 rpm. Its smooth spinning discs used the drag of the moving fluid. The turbine patents were granted in 1913.

timeline.title: Edison Medal
timeline.text: The American Institute of Electrical Engineers awarded him its Edison Medal.

timeline.title: The tower comes down
timeline.text: After Tesla could not pay his debts, the hotel owner who held the mortgage foreclosed and had the tower demolished for scrap. A wartime rumour said the government ordered it, but that was not true.

timeline.title: He tells his own story
timeline.text: His autobiography 'My Inventions' ran as a series in the Electrical Experimenter magazine. It is the source of many stories about his early life.

timeline.title: Last US patent
timeline.text: He received his final US patents, for an aircraft that could take off and land vertically. Wikipedia describes the design as impractical.

timeline.title: 75th birthday
timeline.text: Friends organised a celebration for his 75th birthday. He received congratulations from scientists including Albert Einstein and appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

timeline.title: Death in New York
timeline.text: Tesla died in his room at the Hotel New Yorker at age 86. His archive of over 160,000 documents is now kept at the Nikola Tesla Museum in Belgrade.

patentsNote: Wikipedia's List of Nikola Tesla patents lists 112 US patents (111 numbered patents plus one reissue, RE11,865); the same page says he held at least 278 patents in 26 countries and around 300 worldwide, so many of his patents were foreign. Filing and grant dates here come from each Google Patents record; where Wikipedia shows a different date (US 396,121, 613,809, 655,838, 685,012, 1,061,142 and 1,061,206), Google Patents was used, and a null filing date means Google Patents does not show one.

works.title: AC induction motor
works.text: A motor driven by a rotating magnetic field from alternating current, with no brushes or commutator to spark and wear out (US 381,968).

works.title: A New System of Alternate Current Motors and Transformers
works.text: His May 1888 talk to the American Institute of Electrical Engineers that introduced his motor to engineers.

works.title: Polyphase AC system
works.text: His polyphase motor and transformer patents, licensed by Westinghouse, became the base of the system Westinghouse later sold as the 'Tesla Polyphase System'.

works.title: Tesla coil
works.text: A resonant air-core transformer that makes very high voltage, high frequency current, used in his lighting and wireless work.

works.title: Experiments with Alternate Currents of Very High Frequency and Their Application to Methods of Artificial Illumination
works.text: His 20 May 1891 lecture at Columbia College, where he first showed the Tesla coil in public.

works.title: Experiments with Alternate Currents of High Potential and High Frequency
works.text: His lecture before the Institution of Electrical Engineers in London, later printed as a book.

works.title: On Light and Other High Frequency Phenomena
works.text: Lectures at the Franklin Institute in Philadelphia and in St. Louis, where he spoke of sending signals without wires.

works.title: World's Columbian Exposition
works.text: At the Chicago fair, lit by Westinghouse AC power, he showed wireless lighting and his motors were explained with a spinning copper egg.

works.title: Steam-powered oscillating generator
works.text: A steam-driven piston shook a magnetic armature to make AC directly; it never caught on as a practical generator.

works.title: Radio-controlled boat (telautomaton)
works.text: One of the first wirelessly controlled vehicles, shown at Madison Square Garden and patented as US 613,809.

works.title: Colorado Springs experiments
works.text: High-altitude tests with a giant coil that made artificial lightning, aimed at sending power through the Earth.

works.title: The Problem of Increasing Human Energy
works.text: His long Century Magazine essay of June 1900 on energy, the sun, wireless control and the future.

works.title: Wardenclyffe Tower
works.text: A planned transatlantic wireless station on Long Island that ran out of money, was never finished and was torn down in 1917.

works.title: Bladeless (Tesla) turbine
works.text: A turbine of smooth spinning discs driven by fluid drag, demonstrated in 1906 and patented in 1913 (US 1,061,206).

works.title: My Inventions
works.text: His autobiography, published in six parts in the Electrical Experimenter magazine.

works.title: Valvular conduit (Tesla valve)
works.text: A one-way valve for fluids with no moving parts (US 1,329,559).

works.title: Vertical take-off aircraft
works.text: His last US patents described an aircraft that would take off vertically and then tilt into level flight.
